newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, Hashimoto comment hurts.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, Hashimoto comment hurts.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Monday, hurt by Japan Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's comment that Japan might be tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury bills and buy gold instead.

In a speech delivered at Columbia University in New York, Hashimoto praised the close relationship between Japan and the United States. But responding later to a query about Japan's long-term interest in accumulating U.S. government securities, Hashimoto said stable exchange rates were critical to Japan maintaining its holdings of such instruments.

"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange (rate) stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," said Hashimoto in a question and answer session carried live by Reuters Financial Television.

In the U.S. Treasury market, which was flat to a bit higher in mid-afternoon, prices slipped when the comment was reported. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slid about 1/4 of a point after the Hashimoto comment.
The bond closed at 99-8/32, down 8/32, to yield 6.68 percent versus Friday's closing yield of 6.66 percent.
The fact that the comment was made just ahead of the Treasury's monthly auctions of two- and five-year notes was one reason that it made an impression, analysts said.
The Treasury will sell $15.5 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $11.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.

"The market was more susceptible to Hashimoto's comments because they occurred just before the Treasury's two-year note auction," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "If you're going to have to buy the two-years, you'd like to see them cheapen up a little bit."
The short end of the maturity curve also weakened.

The Treasury sold $14.0 billion in three- and six-month bills at its weekly bill auction on Monday at rates of 4.94 percent and 5.05 percent, respectively. After the auction results were announced, bill rates rose sharply. On the three- and six-month bills sold on Monday, rates on a when-issued basis ended at 4.99 percent and 5.07 percent, respectively.

Another reason the Hashimoto comments made a mark is that they were made when a consensus seemed to have formed that the bond market had gone as high as it could go without more evidence that the economy grew at a slower pace in June.

Data on June, so far, is very limited and a more comprehensive picture of the June economy will not be available until next week when the National Association of Purchasing Managment (NAPM) releases its index and the U.S. Labor Department releases its June employment report.

"As long as there's a possibility that the Federal Reserve will be out there with a rate hike later this year, the upside is very limited from here," said Bill Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. "The two-year note yield has had real difficulty trying to go below six percent and I think that will be the case going forward."
Before the Hashimoto comment, participants characterized trading session as "deadly dull" with the two- and five-year note auctions being the primary focus.

"Flows were light and non-descript," said Youngdahl. He said the five-year note auction on Wednesday could get support from investors in short maturities "reaching for yield" in the middle of the maturity curve.
Five-year notes finished at 100-28/32, down 2/32 to yield 6.29 percent on Monday. Ten-year notes ended at 101-21/32, down 3/32, to yield 6.40 percent.
At the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 100-13/32, down 1/32 to yield 6.02 percent.
Three-month bill rates rose eight basis points to 5.02 percent and six-month bill rates rose two basis points to 5.10 percent. Year bill rates finished unchanged at 5.34 percent.
